tholosan-ut-magorum-et-maleficiorum-erro:

emerson-nature-1836:

pushkin-captains-daughter-1836:

gogol-inspector-general-1836:

miller-evidence-second-coming-1836:

buchner-leonce-lena-lenz-1836:

butler-analogy-religion-1736:

On 19 June 1862 Roest van Limburg wrote again to Secretary of State William H. Seward, ten days after the first burst of Dutch notes. His letter is Document 536 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

The mid-June note shows the Dutch business settling into its longer rhythm after the intense first week. Van Limburg continued to represent a government whose ships, colonies, and carrying trade gave it a permanent interest in American maritime practice. Seward's department dealt with The Hague on two tracks, through Pike abroad and Van Limburg at home. The letter belongs to the home track, where questions arrived in writing and were answered in kind, on the record.
frus-1862-d636:
On 8 May 1861 Townsend Harris addressed this dispatch from Japan to the Secretary of State, by then William H. Seward in the new Lincoln administration. It is Document 636 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Harris wrote a month after Fort Sumter, though no word of the war could yet have reached him. His subject was Japan. There he remained the solitary American minister. The address to the office rather than the man suits a dispatch sent across a change of government. His reports from Edo in 1861 describe a treaty system still fragile and a minister worn by isolation and ill health. The letter opens the Civil War-era Japanese file in the volume.
frus-1863p1-d36:
On 14 August 1862, Judah P. Benjamin wrote to A. Dudley Mann. Benjamin ran the Confederate state office in Richmond; Mann was one of the South's first agents sent to win backing in Europe. The letter is document 36 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Mann had roamed the courts of Europe since 1861, seeking a nod for the South's cause. Benjamin's letters kept such agents stocked with claims, facts, and hope. This one predates the others in its group, a look at the South's pitch in the summer of 1862. Printed in the Union's volume, it lets readers hear the other side in its own words.
frus-1863p1-d136:
On 28 March 1863, William H. Seward sent this second letter of the day to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 136 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

A same-day Adams letter sits right after this one in the volume, so the pens crossed in print as they did at sea. Seward's second sheet of 28 March held its own head of the brief, as his pairs always did. Adams would read it ten days on, beside the news of the hour. The letter is a stitch in the tightest-woven part of the file, the spring of 1863.
frus-1863p1-d236:
To guide his minister in London, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote these orders on 14 July 1863 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. They stand as document 236 of the 1863 volume. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

The chief aim behind such orders was simple: keep Britain from treating the Confederacy as a nation. Every instruction from Washington served that goal in some way. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d336:
On 10 December 1862, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It appears as document 336 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Cases in these notes can look small, one ship or one arrested man, yet each tested the rules of neutrality. Both governments treated the precedents as serious business. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d436:
Secretary William H. Seward wrote this official letter to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington on 1 April 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d536:
Dated 27 May 1863, document 536 is a letter from F. W. Seward to Lord Lyons. F. W. Seward was the Assistant Secretary of State, writing here to Britain's minister in Washington. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d636:
Among the day's business on 8 October 1863 was a letter from Charles Francis Adams to William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. Adams in London was the Union's front line in Britain, pressing its case with the British government week after week.

Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. Adams's task was to make the Union's case where it counted, inside the British capital, while Seward set the line from Washington. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
plos-pbio-0020036:
Eric L. Snyder, Bryan R. Meade, Cheryl C. Saenz, and co-workers tested a bold cancer treatment in PLOS Biology in 2004. Peritoneal carcinomatosis is cancer spread across the belly lining, often from ovarian cancer. It resists standard chemotherapy and has a grim outlook.

Their approach uses a peptide, a short protein chain, that can cross into cells and switch on p53. p53 is a guard protein that can push damaged cells to die. Turning it on inside spread tumor cells offers a way to attack the disease at many sites at once. The study is an early proof of concept. It points to cell-penetrating peptides as a delivery route worth refining.
plos-pbio-0020336:
Elise R. Hondorp and Rowena G. Matthews studied a stress weak point in E. coli in PLOS Biology in 2004. The bacterium makes the amino acid methionine with an enzyme called MetE. That enzyme does not need vitamin B12, which makes it valuable when B12 is scarce.

Oxidative stress switches MetE off, the team found, halting methionine supply. The cell must then lean on its B12-based backup enzyme or stop growing. That fragility looks like a design flaw, yet it may serve as a stress sensor. Either way, the result shows how a single enzyme can link air, diet, and growth. It also marks a possible target: germs that depend on MetE could be starved by stress-like drugs.
plos-pone-0000136:
Yongli Zhang, Abbye E. McEwen, Donald M. Crothers, and colleagues published this biophysics paper in PLOS ONE in 2006. It studies the Lac repressor, a bacterial protein that switches genes off by gripping DNA and bending it into a loop. The authors analyze this repression inside living cells through the mechanics of the loop itself.

DNA looping is a common way cells control genes, but it is hard to measure in vivo. The authors use the physics of loop formation to explain how strongly the repressor shuts its target genes down. The work links molecular mechanics to gene control, a bridge between physics and genetics.
plos-pone-0000236:
Selma Ugurel, Ranjit K. Thirumaran, Sandra Bloethner, and colleagues published this melanoma study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Two genes, B-RAF and N-RAS, are often mutated in skin cancer. The authors report that these mutations are preserved when tumor cells are grown for a short time in vitro, and that they affect prognosis differently.

Cell lines are only useful models if they keep the tumor's key mutations. This study checks that they do, over short propagation. It also compares what each mutation means for patient outlook. Both points help researchers who use cultured melanoma cells to test drugs.
plos-pone-0000336:
Laurin J. Kasehagen, Ivo Mueller, Benson Kiniboro, and colleagues published this malaria genetics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. The Duffy blood group protein is the door Plasmodium vivax uses to enter red blood cells; people who lack it were thought immune. In Papua New Guinea, the authors report reduced vivax infection in Duffy-negative heterozygotes, people with one copy of the negative variant.

Partial protection in heterozygotes is a subtler picture than total immunity. The finding refines who is at risk of vivax malaria in PNG, where the parasite is common. It also speaks to how this host-parasite relationship is evolving in real populations.
plos-pone-0000436:
Bora E. Baysal reported a recurring mutation found where it was not expected, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The change is a stop-codon mutation in the gene for succinate dehydrogenase subunit B. That protein is part of the cell's energy machinery. Mutations in it are known from certain tumors. Baysal found the same change in normal peripheral blood and in childhood T-cell acute leukemia samples.

A stop codon ends a protein early, usually crippling it. Finding such a change in healthy blood raises questions: is it a harmless inherited variant, an early step toward disease, or an artifact? The paper's value is in flagging the recurrence so others can test what it means.
plos-pone-0000536:
Simon Melov and colleagues connected a signature of brain aging to energy stress in cells, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Tau is a brain protein that becomes hyperphosphorylated, overloaded with phosphate tags, in Alzheimer's disease, where it tangles. The team showed that mitochondrial oxidative stress causes hyperphosphorylation of tau.

Mitochondria are the cell's power plants, and oxidative stress is the damage from their chemical exhaust. Linking that stress directly to tau's change puts failing energy production upstream of a hallmark of Alzheimer's. The finding supports treatments aimed at protecting mitochondria as a way to slow the disease's molecular cascade.
plos-pone-0000636:
Otto Appenzeller, Clifford Qualls, Franca Barbic and co-authors read body rhythms in hair and teeth for PLOS ONE in 2007. Biological rhythms offer insight into normal physiology and disease. They can also serve as biomarkers, measurable signs, in nerve degeneration. Hair and teeth grow in layers, locking in chemical records over time.

The team presents a diverse data set showing stable isotope ratios in these tissues reflect those rhythms. An isotope ratio is the balance between heavier and lighter forms of an element. If tissues keep an extended rhythm record, a strand of hair becomes a timeline. Clinicians could read past physiology from samples that are easy to collect and store.
plos-pone-0000736:
Jeffrey A. Gold, Yoshihiko Hoshino, Marcus B. Jones and colleagues reported a cautionary result on immune therapy for anthrax, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Bacillus anthracis causes inhalational anthrax and can live inside host cells. Even with appropriate antibiotics, mortality from inhaled anthrax approaches 45 percent, underscoring the need for better added therapies. Interferons are immune signals that might seem natural helpers.

Their title states the opposite: giving interferon-alpha and interferon-gamma increased lethality in mice with inhalational anthrax. A therapy that harms instead of helps is vital to know before human use. Negative findings of this clarity protect patients and redirect research.
plos-pone-0000836:
Giulia Somenzi, Giusy Sala, Stefano Rossetti and colleagues showed that vitamin A's active form has two faces, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Retinoic acid, the bioactive derivative of vitamin A, controls transcription through its receptors and exerts a potent antiproliferative effect on human cells. Yet a number of studies show retinoic acid can also promote cell survival and growth. The contradiction needed a mechanism.

By disrupting retinoic acid receptor alpha, the team reveals the growth promoter face of retinoic acid. One receptor apparently carries the brake, while other routes carry growth signals. Separating the faces matters for retinoid drugs in cancer, where pushing growth would be the worst outcome.
plos-pone-0000936:
Zhike Zi and Edda Klipp modeled a major cell signaling route with both constraints and kinetics, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The TGF-beta pathway helps control growth, cell death and specialization. Getting its dynamics right is central to understanding how cells decide their fate.

The authors combine constraint based modeling, which sets the bounds of what a system can do, with kinetic analysis, which follows rates over time. Their target is the Smad dependent branch of the pathway. A model that matches real timing can predict how a cell answers a signal of a given strength. Such predictions guide experiments on cancer and development alike.
plos-pone-0001036:
Jeremy Peirce, Karl Broman, Lu Lu and colleagues offered a simple way to merge gene mapping data from many crosses, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Linkage studies mark chromosome stretches that affect a trait. For many traits, enough separate studies now exist that combining them could sharpen the locations and reveal new ones.

Different crosses and study designs, though, resist simple pooling. The authors present a method for combining such data across experiments. Sharper trait locations mean fewer candidate genes to test by hand. For traits like disease risk or behavior, that narrowing is the step that turns a map into a gene.
plos-pone-0001136:
DNA methylation is a chemical mark that helps control which genes are active. Most marks sit in a symmetrical pattern called CpG, but a smaller share fall in lopsided, non-CpG patterns. Valérie Grandjean, Ruken Yaman, and François Cuzin asked how those odd marks get established, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article.

Their title gives the core finding. An inherited epigenetic mark requires the enzyme DNA methyltransferase 1 to set up a complex pattern of non-CpG methylation from scratch. Epigenetic marks can pass between generations without changing the DNA code itself. The study clarifies how one such mark is written.
plos-pone-0001236:
Scrapie is a fatal brain disease of sheep, and some prion protein variants make sheep susceptible to it. Rami Sawalha and colleagues report a paradox in a 2007 PLOS ONE article: lambs carrying the susceptible genotypes survived better after birth. Susceptibility alleles persist at high frequencies in many flocks despite centuries of selection against them.

That persistence suggests the alleles bring some benefit, or hitchhike with one. The authors' survival finding offers a candidate benefit in early life. It complicates eradication programs based on breeding for resistance, since removing the alleles might remove the advantage too.
plos-pone-0001336:
Learning a new movement, like reaching in an altered force field, uses feedback from vision and from the body's own position sense. David Franklin and colleagues asked whether vision is actually necessary for such learning, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Humans integrate multi-modal sensory feedback to adjust movements and complete tasks successfully.

The authors report, as their title states, that visual feedback is not necessary for the learning of novel dynamics. Proprioception, the sense of limb position, can carry the learning alone. The result reshapes accounts of motor learning that put vision in charge.
plos-pone-0001436:
Rhiannon Biddick, G. Lynn Law, and Elton Young published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on two yeast gene switches. The two switches jointly run many genes that sugar normally keeps off. The team set out to split their roles. They asked which one calls in helper proteins and reshapes the DNA wrapping at each gene.

By testing each switch alone, they gave each a distinct share of the work. One led on some steps, the other on the rest. Fine splits like this show how cells share tasks between like factors. The work grounds models of how yeast adapts when its food source changes.
plos-pone-0001536:
Daphne Ling, Laura Flores, and Lee Riley wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE review of lab tests for lung TB. Hundreds of studies grade tests that copy TB DNA from spit samples. Store bought tests gave more steady results than home built ones. Past pooled reviews found high truth for negatives but shaky rates for spotting cases.

The authors pool the data again and probe what drives the spread in results. Their work gives clinics a firmer read on what these tests can and cannot do. In poor lands where TB is rife, that read guides scarce funds. It also sets bars for the next wave of tests.
plos-pone-0001636:
Navjot S. Sodhi, David Bickford, Arvin C. Diesmos, and their co-authors weighed the causes of the worldwide loss of frogs and other amphibians in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Habitat loss, climate change, over-hunting, and disease have all been blamed. What was not clear is how much each cause counts, and how they act together.

The authors describe their study as the largest global look at the problem to that date. The full text gives the data they gathered across species and regions, and their ranking of the drivers of decline and extinction. Amphibians are often the first group hit by damage to fresh water and land habitats. A clear ranking helps conservation groups decide where effort and money will do the most good.
plos-pone-0001736:
Douglas J. Blackiston, Elena Silva Casey, and Martha R. Weiss asked whether a moth remembers its caterpillar lessons, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Insects with complete metamorphosis rebuild their bodies wholesale, changing both form and lifestyle. Whether larval experience can persist through pupation into adulthood was an open question.

The team trained caterpillars, let them transform, and tested the adult moths for retained learning. They also assessed two mechanisms that could carry memory through the rebuild. The full text gives the training, the adult tests, and the verdict. If memory survives a near-total body rebuild, that says something deep about where memories live in a nervous system.
plos-pone-0001836:
Michael Roberts, Aleksey V. Zimin, Wayne Hayes, and their co-authors improved genome assembly software in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The assembly methods used for whole-genome shotgun data have a major impact on the quality of resulting draft genomes. Shotgun sequencing reads a genome in millions of fragments that software must overlap and join.

Their algorithm generates a set of 'reliable' overlaps by identifying repeat k-mers. Those are short repeated sequences that cause false joins, and the method improves Phrap-based assembly of the rat genome. The full text gives the algorithm and the before-and-after assembly quality. Every genome project of the era depended on such assembly hygiene; one repeat mishandled can scramble whole chromosomes.
plos-pone-0001936:
Johan Rebetz and co-authors compared brain tumor cells to stem cells in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Gliomas are the most common brain tumors, and they range from slow low-grade forms to fast high-grade ones. Some tumor cells act like stem or progenitor cells, the early cells that can grow into many types, and such cells may drive the tumor.

The team took live glioma cells and checked how far they match that early-cell pattern. They also tracked a marker called CD133, and the cells' power to take on nerve-cell traits. High-grade tumors showed more of both. The work may help doctors judge how a tumor will act.
plos-pone-0002036:
Annemarie Surlykke and Elisabeth Kalko measured how loud hunting bats call, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Bats that hunt by echolocation have spread across many habitats and prey types. Much past work charted how the pitch pattern of their calls fits each habitat and hunting style. How loud the calls are had drawn far less study.

As the title states, these bats cry out loud to detect their prey. Loud calls carry farther and return stronger echoes from small insects. Volume, it turns out, is as tuned a part of the bat's sonar as pitch.
plos-pone-0002136:
Matthew Ward, Serkan Erdin, Tuan Tran, and co-authors tackled a pile-up problem in protein science, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Labs keep solving the shapes of proteins whose jobs are unknown, and the list grows faster than anyone can test them one by one. Guessing a protein's job usually means comparing it with proteins whose jobs are known.

The authors asked whether those comparisons get sharper when they focus on the structural features that evolution has kept most stable. By comparing such features in both directions, they aimed to give unknown proteins a family and a likely role. Better guesses mean lab tests can start closer to the truth.
plos-pone-0002236:
Laura Fontana, Micol Fiori, Sonia Albini, and co-authors blocked a small RNA to fight stubborn neuroblastoma, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Neuroblastoma is a childhood cancer of nerve tissue, and some tumors resist therapy. The team had traced a key pathway: the cancer gene MYCN, when overactive, switches on a cluster of microRNAs that includes miR-17-5p.

Those microRNAs suppress two protective proteins, p21 and BIM, letting tumor cells grow unchecked. Blocking miR-17-5p with an antagomir, a molecule built to silence it, abolished the growth of therapy-resistant neuroblastoma in their tests. The result nominates one small RNA as a drug target in a hard cancer.
plos-pone-0002336:
Riffat Naseem and Michelle Webb examined how the breast cancer protein BRCA1 binds DNA, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. BRCA1 helps maintain the integrity of the genome; when it fails, breast and ovarian cancer risk climbs sharply. The exact mechanisms of its guard work remain unclear, despite years of study.

BRCA1 can bind DNA directly, hinting at a hands-on role at the genome itself. The authors analyzed that binding activity and how the tumor suppressor p53, another genome guardian, modulates it. Two famous protective proteins interacting at DNA may explain part of their shared defense, and why losing either opens the door to cancer.
plos-pone-0002436:
Dahiya and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Neetu Dahiya, Cheryl A. Sherman-Baust, Tian-Li Wang, and others. Its subject is microRNA Expression and Identification of Putative miRNA Targets in Ovarian Cancer. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) represent a class of small non-coding RNAs that control gene expression by targeting mRNAs and triggering either translation repression or RNA degradation.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002536:
Led by Inderjit, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Inderjit, Jarrod L. Pollock, Ragan M. Callaway, and others. Its subject is phytotoxic Effects of (±)-Catechin In vitro , in Soil, and in the Field. Exploring the residence time of allelochemicals released by plants into different soils, episodic exposure of plants to allelochemicals.

Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002636:
Work by Yimin Wu and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was phase 1 trial of malaria transmission blocking vaccine candidates pfs25 and pvs25 formulated with montanide ISA 51. Authorship is credited in the record to Yimin Wu and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Pfs25 and Pvs25, surface proteins of mosquito stage of the malaria parasites P. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002736:
Research from Simone Köhler and co-authors, published in PLOS ONE in 2008, covers rheological characterization of the bundling transition in F-Actin solutions induced by methylcellulose. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Simone Köhler, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. In many in vitro experiments Brownian motion hampers quantitative data analysis. The authors add a further point. Therefore, additives are widely used to increase the solvent viscosity. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002836:
Work by Anders F. Andersson and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008, dealing with comparative analysis of human gut microbiota by barcoded pyrosequencing. The catalog record names Anders F. Andersson first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Humans host complex microbial communities believed to contribute to health maintenance and, when in imbalance, to the development of diseases. The authors add a further point. Determining the microbial composition in patients and healthy controls may thus provide novel therapeutic targets. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002936:
Edwin Michael, Mwele Malecela, Mihail Zervos and co-authors weighed chronic disease care in filariasis eradication in 2008. The global program aimed to end lymphatic filariasis by halting transmission with four to six years of yearly mass drug doses. Costs and management hurdles stood in the way.

Writing in PLOS ONE, they argue for the value of caring for people already living with chronic disease as part of elimination programs. Such care builds trust and keeps communities engaged with drug rounds. The paper speaks to program leaders balancing a finish-line goal against duties to those already harmed.
plos-pone-0003036:
Nora Khaldi and Kenneth Wolfe asked in 2008 where the extra genes of Aspergillus oryzae came from. Sequencing showed this fungus carries about 20 percent more genes than its relatives A. nidulans and A. fumigatus. Such a surplus demands an origin story: duplication, transfer, or something else.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the authors evaluate several possible causes of the elevated gene number. The origins proved elusive, as their title admits. A. oryzae is the mold behind sake and soy sauce fermentations, so its genome history has both industrial and evolutionary interest. The article appeared in PLOS ONE, an open access journal anyone can read free online.
plos-pone-0003136:
Francesca Luca, Giuseppina Bubba, Massimo Basile and colleagues survey variation in the NAT2 gene in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Differences at NAT2 have long been known to change how well people break down a wide range of drugs used in care. The team explored the pattern of that variation in twelve human populations, extending both the map range and the detail of past work.

Their title reports that several amino acid variants in NAT2 look advantageous. Readers get a broad human picture of a gene that shapes drug response. The study may help explain why the same dose can act quite differently in different people and groups.
plos-pone-0003236:
Raik Rönicke, Anja Klemm, Jessica Meinhardt and colleagues question a standard toxicity assay in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The MTT reduction assay is a frequently used and easily reproducible method to measure beta-amyloid toxicity in different types of single cell culture. To the authors' knowledge, the influence of beta-amyloid on MTT reduction itself had not been examined as a possible artefact.

Their title asks whether A-beta mediated diminution of MTT reduction is an artefact of single cell culture. Readers get a methods warning with broad reach, since the assay is used in many labs. If the measure is flawed, many past toxicity readings may need a second look.
plos-pone-0003336:
Chang-Ching Yang, Yang-Hsin Shih, Miau-Hwa Ko and colleagues transplant umbilical stem cells in rats in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Human umbilical mesenchymal stem cells isolated from Wharton's jelly of the umbilical cord can be easily obtained and processed compared with embryonic or bone marrow stem cells. These cells may be a valuable source in repair of spinal cord injury. The team examine effects after complete transection of the rat spinal cord.

Readers get a test of an accessible cell source in the hardest spinal injury model, full cutting of the cord. Any benefit there is notable, though rat recovery often exceeds what patients achieve.
plos-pone-0007436: Fruit flies fight viruses with a defense pathway called Imd, previously thought to handle only bacteria. This study infected flies with cricket paralysis virus and found the Imd pathway switching on to battle it. Proving flies use this same alarm system against viruses widens what the simple fly can teach us about immunity.
plos-pone-0007536: Human episodic memory — remembering what happened — may run on the brain's theta rhythm. This study built a computer model in which the timing of neuron firing against that rhythm predicts memory formation. The model turns a phenomenon seen in rats into a testable theory of how people encode their past.
plos-pone-0007636: Milk-making cells from dairy cows are hard to study without a reliable lab model. This study established a mammary cell line from a lactating Chinese Holstein cow and characterized its behavior in culture. The new line gives researchers a stable window into bovine milk biology.
plos-pone-0007736: The stomach bacterium H. pylori causes ulcers and cancer, and its CagA protein is a chief suspect. This study correlated variations in CagA's tail region with different diseases across strains. The tail's sequence helps predict whether an infection turns dangerous.
plos-pone-0007836: Bird flu H5N1 must bind human airway cells to spark a pandemic. This study identified mutations in the virus's hemagglutinin that confer binding to human tracheal epithelium. Watching for these mutations is watching for the next pandemic's opening move.
plos-pone-0007936: The gene silencers REST and CoREST sculpt the developing nervous system. This study showed they modulate which neuronal subtypes form, how they mature, and how they are maintained. The pair act as master editors of brain-cell identity.
plos-pone-0008036: Star traders' risk-adjusted returns got a reality check. A 2009 PLOS ONE note by Coates and Page examined trader Sharpe ratios, the money made per unit of risk. The efficient-market view says little edge should persist. The analysis of real trading records tests whether skill or luck drives the numbers.
plos-pone-0008136: Seizure drugs work differently in males and females — even in flies. This study built a fly model of chronic pentylenetetrazole-induced behavioral deficit and found gender differences in the transcriptomic response. The tiny model flags sex as a variable in epilepsy.
plos-pone-0008236: Two plant genes were found job-sharing hormone control. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Zhang's team showed AtSOFL1 and AtSOFL2 redundantly tune cytokinin levels in Arabidopsis. Cytokinins steer plant growth, but their regulation was murky. Knocking out one gene did little; losing both mattered. The backup arrangement reveals how plants safeguard their hormone balance.
plos-pone-0008336: A biofuel grass was checked as a pest haven. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Spencer and Raghu asked whether Miscanthus x giganteus shelters a major maize pest. The tall grass is eyed for Corn Belt biofuel plots. If it harbors the pest, the fuel crop could backfire. The refuge-or-reservoir test informs planting decisions.
plos-pone-0008436: Cystic fibrosis cells showed a rewired death cascade. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Kerbiriou's team found the calpain-caspase-12-caspase-3 death chain runs differently in F508del-CFTR cells. The misfolded channel protein stresses the ER. The altered cascade changes how the cells die. The rewiring suggests new angles on CF cell fate.
plos-pone-0008536: A blood protein was found blocking brain tumors. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Kärrlander's team showed histidine-rich glycoprotein prevents mouse glioblastoma. The protein starves tumors of vessels. The anti-angiogenic effect was the key. The finding nominates a natural tumor brake.
plos-pone-0008636: Termites' wood-digesting enzymes got a family tree. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Todaka's team analyzed cellulolytic enzyme genes across termite lineages and a related cockroach. Gut protists do the digesting. The gene phylogeny reveals the partnership's history. The tree informs biofuel research.
plos-pone-0008736: Prostate cancer's germ link got a big-test check. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Cheng's team probed prostate inflammation and sex-germ links to prostate cancer in California men. The swelling-cancer link was tested. The check refines risk science.
